# Introduction

Branching processes describe how individual cases give rise to further
infections and provide the natural generative model for the early phase of an
outbreak, before depletion of susceptibles comes to dominate the dynamics
[CITE: Farrington 1999; Lloyd-Smith 2005; Blumberg & Lloyd-Smith 2013].
A parent case produces offspring according to an offspring distribution, each
offspring in turn produces its own offspring, and the chain terminates when no
further infections occur.
The mean of the offspring distribution is the reproduction number, while its
dispersion captures the heterogeneity in onward transmission that drives
superspreading and chain extinction.
The timing of transmission within the infectious period of a parent adds a
survival structure on top of this branching skeleton, and interventions act on
the timing or on the offspring count to alter who infects whom.

Several R packages implement variants of this model for specific outbreak
analyses.
`ringbp` simulates ring-based containment of contact-traced outbreaks
[CITE: Hellewell 2020], `epichains` computes chain-size and chain-length
distributions and their likelihoods [CITE: epichains], and `superspreading`
estimates offspring overdispersion from chain-size data
[CITE: superspreading].
`simulist` simulates outbreak line lists with attached natural-history
information for software testing and downstream analysis [CITE: simulist], and
`pepbp` models post-exposure prophylaxis in ring vaccination
[CITE: Meakin 2024 / pepbp].
Each of these packages addresses its target question well, and most are
actively maintained by the same community.
However, they share the same mathematical core, namely an offspring
distribution, a generation-time distribution and an intervention layer, and
each reimplements it for whichever analysis it addresses.

The cost of this duplication is largely operational.
An analyst combining simulation, analytical likelihoods and intervention
modelling within a single outbreak response has to switch between tools,
reconcile parameter conventions and intervention semantics across them and
write glue code that the underlying mathematics does not require.
Rapid recomposition under the time pressure of a response then becomes harder
than it should be: a scenario that adds isolation on top of an existing
simulation may need a different package from the one used for the original
chain-size fit, and intervention parameters in one package may not have direct
equivalents in another.
The 2026 Ebola virus disease outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo,
where transmission of *Bundibugyo ebolavirus* required rapid parameter refits
and intervention scenario sweeps within days of the outbreak being declared,
made this cost concrete for our team.

EpiBranch.jl unifies the offspring draw, transmission timing and
competing-risks resolution behind a single dispatched interface in Julia, and
treats interventions, host attributes and observation models as first-class
composable components.
A model is here understood as the whole generative specification of how data
arise, that is a transmission process, the population it acts on, the policy in
force and how cases are observed.
The same model object answers both what the model could produce, through
`simulate`, and how likely observed data were, through `loglikelihood`.
The two entry points cannot disagree.
Where closed-form chain-size distributions exist
[CITE: Borel; Farrington gborel; epichains] they plug in by dispatch and
inherit gradient-based inference, while the remaining cases fall back to
simulation with gradient-free samplers.
Composition with other Julia probabilistic programming packages, including the
renewal-process modelling in EpiAware.jl [CITE: EpiAware], works through
Turing.jl submodels [CITE: Turing; Fjelde 2025] without changes to either
package.
We implement the package in Julia rather than R because the type system
supports the dispatched composition on which the design rests, and because the
Julia probabilistic programming ecosystem provides the submodel interfaces that
the cross-package composition relies on.

The remainder of this paper sets out the design (@sec-design), the
composability properties that follow from it (@sec-composability), the duality
between analytical and simulation-based approaches and its connection to
survival analysis (@sec-duality and @sec-survival), and operational use in the
2026 Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (@sec-drc).

# Design {#sec-design}

## Design principles

Five principles govern what enters the package and where its seams fall.

1. *Simple but rigorous.*
   The aim is to express only what the analyses we conduct require, and a new
   mechanism earns its place only when an analysis cannot be done without it.
   Where a closed-form likelihood and a simulation-based one are both
   available and equivalent, the closed form is preferred.
   A single verb performs the dispatch (`loglikelihood` to score data,
   `simulate` to generate it), and no family of wrapper functions is needed
   for each data type or model variant.

2. *Self-explanatory.*
   Type and function names should, as far as possible, match the intuition
   that the epidemiology already supplies.
   Mathematical names such as `Borel` and `GammaBorel` are appropriate where
   they match the literature a user is likely to come from, whereas
   operational names should read the way the epidemiology describes what is
   happening.
   If a public name can only be understood by reading the source, it is
   generally the wrong name.

3. *Cleanly separable concerns.*
   The process model, observation model, data, inference, simulation and
   output each own one thing behind an explicit interface.
   A new alternative, such as a network process, multi-stream observation,
   time-varying reporting or aggregated counts, can then be
   introduced by implementing the relevant interface, and each concern
   remains replaceable on its own.

4. *Extensible from outside.*
   A transmission model, observation model, intervention or data type can be
   added from a separate package or a single script while reusing the whole
   framework infrastructure, and the contracts that such a component has to
   satisfy are documented and small.

5. *Documented with examples.*
   Every public extension point comes with a worked example, and the
   tutorials are executed when the documentation is built, which stops the
   prose drifting from the code.
   Without this, the previous principle is empty.

We judge the architecture set out below against these five principles, and
return to them whenever anything substantial is added.

## The model as a generative specification

A model in EpiBranch.jl is the whole generative account of how data arise,
built by composing a transmission process with the modelling layers that force
and observe it.
The transmission process is the between-host mechanism alone, that is how
infection passes from one host to the next, and it carries nothing else.
Onto this we compose four further layers:

- *disease*: the within-host natural history, or the timed states a case moves
  through (latent, infectious, symptom onset, severe, recovered or died), with
  treatment expressible as a state it may pass through;
- *attributes*: who the people are (age, susceptibility, infectiousness),
  which can bear on transmission, on the disease course and on how
  interventions find their targets;
- *interventions*: what is done about it (isolation, contact tracing,
  vaccination);
- *observation*: how cases come to be seen (under-reporting, reporting
  delays).

Together with the process, these five parts correspond to the way in which
epidemiology usually decomposes an outbreak, in which a pathogen spreads,
infection causes disease, in a population of people, under a response, watched
through surveillance.
Keeping them distinct allows each to be replaced on its own, and allows the
same layer to sit on any process.
An isolation policy that truncates infectiousness in a homogeneous branching
process, for example, is the same object when the process underneath it is a
network.

Both entry points read the composed model rather than the bare process.
`simulate` answers the question of what the model could produce and
`loglikelihood` the question of how likely observed data were, and because
both consume the same composition they cannot disagree.
A simulation-based likelihood therefore reproduces the same generative
specification that produced the data.
In particular, this matters where interventions are present, as the likelihood
of a set of observed chain sizes is only correct if the composition that
scores them applies the same isolation that suppressed transmission in the
observed outbreak.
A scenario sweep is then a map over compositions, each scenario being the same
process under a different response, and a counterfactual is a fresh
composition carrying the layer of interest.
We deliberately provide no helper for swapping a single input in place, and the
layers of a model always remain explicit.

These layers are not independent of one another.
Attributes can bear on transmission, disease and intervention targeting at
once, the infectious window is defined by disease states, and a transmission
rate expressed as a reproduction number depends on the mean infectious period.
Composing the layers gives each of them access to the others it needs, and
resolves these couplings once both sides are in hand.
A structure-driven process, for example, derives its infectious window, and
where transmission is given as a reproduction number also its rate, from the
composed disease layer at the moment the model is simulated or scored.
The process then stays purely the transmission, and the disease remains a
single, separately specified layer.

## Three separated stages

The engine resolves every potential transmission in three stages, of which
only the first is specific to the model.

### Stage 1: offspring draw

This stage is the pure branching process, with no time and no interventions in
it.
For a given parent, contacts are drawn from an offspring distribution, either
as a single count or as a count per type in a multi-type model.
The reproduction number $R$ and the overdispersion $k$ are properties of that
distribution, and where a contact matrix is supplied it sets the mixing pattern
across types.
A transmission model defines this stage and nothing else, and it can do so in
one of two ways.
An *offspring-driven* model, that is the branching process and its variants,
can produce its candidates one parent at a time and returns a count.
A *structure-driven* model, such as a network, household or metapopulation
process, cannot do this, because a susceptible may be reachable by several
infectious neighbours in the same generation and infections deplete a fixed
pool.
Instead, such a model names the candidate contacts that each infectious node
reaches, and the engine resolves a node reached several times in one generation
only once.
The network process in the companion `EpiNetwork.jl` package is the worked
example.
Either way, the model only says who contacts whom.

### Stage 2: timing

Each candidate is given a potential transmission time drawn from the
infectiousness profile of the parent, that is the generation-time
distribution.
That distribution can be fixed or constructed per individual, and the timing
can read any per-individual quantity, for example the incubation period of the
parent or anything that the attributes layer has stored.
In the language of survival analysis, this stage supplies the hazard $h(t)$.

### Stage 3: competing risks

Each candidate is resolved to infected or not by a single per-pair decision
composed from a list of risk sources.
Parent infectiousness and contact susceptibility are not privileged checks in
the engine but default risk sources on the same surface that an intervention
uses, and isolation truncation, or any other risk that an intervention
contributes, joins the same list.
A model can also contribute sources here, for a transmission term that belongs
to the edge rather than to either node.
A per-edge probability in a network model is perhaps the most obvious example,
as per-node
susceptibility and infectiousness cannot carry a per-pair quantity without
forcing one shared value across all the edges of a node.
A contact is infected only if no risk blocks it, and the earliest removal
before the transmission time of a contact wins without the engine taking an
explicit minimum.

Contacts that fail a check are still stored.
They are contacts that were made but did not transmit, and they carry the
contact-tracing table and the accounting of intervention effort (contacts
traced, vaccines administered, tests used) without separate bookkeeping.

### Why the separation matters

Keeping the first stage free of time and policy opens the model to analysis.
Because the offspring draw is a pure probabilistic object, standard tools apply
to it, such as the extinction probability from the dominant
eigenvalue of the offspring mean, chain-size distributions and analytical
likelihoods.
None of these depends on timing or on interventions, and the draw remains
differentiable wherever the distribution permits.
Interventions instead act on the timing and competing-risks stages, where
isolation truncates the hazard, contact tracing moves the truncation earlier
and vaccination lowers susceptibility.
Because the generation-time CDF evaluated at an intervention time is the
survival function, the same objects appear in simulation and in the pairwise
likelihood of @kenah2008, and intervention effectiveness can be estimated from
observed generation times using the same quantities that were used to simulate
them (@sec-survival).

## Extension by dispatch

We add new behaviour by defining a new type and a method on it.
If one wants a variant, it should generally be enough to write a small struct
and one or two methods, without editing the package source and without copying
the body of an existing function.
A `Union` field whose members trigger different branches, a `Symbol` that
switches behaviour inside a function or a `Bool` that selects a policy are all
signs that a seam sits in the wrong place and should instead become a type that
is dispatched on.

This holds on every axis.
Spatial, network and immunity dynamics enter as new model subtypes or as
reusable wrapper types.
Interventions are largely orchestrators of smaller dispatched pieces.
An intervention struct is a thin shell wiring together independently dispatched
components (eligibility, rate, delay and effect), each of which is a type with
a method, and the body of the intervention holds no hardcoded policy
branching.
Composition then operates at two levels, between the interventions that a model
carries and within the pieces of each intervention.
We express time-dependent policies by wrapping an intervention in a schedule,
and no intervention needs its own start-time field.
The gate applies to the time of the action, and an individual infected before a
policy begins can still be affected if the time at which they would be tested
falls after it.
Output, observation and outcome rules take the same shape, and mortality,
hospitalisation, reporting, stopping conditions and line-list columns are all
typed objects with methods.
The test we apply to any component is whether a plausible new variant can be
added without editing the source of that component, and where it cannot, the
varying part is lifted into a trait that is dispatched on.

Each individual carries a small typed core that the engine reads, holding its
place in the transmission tree, its infection time and the two universal
modifiers of susceptibility and infectiousness, alongside an open dictionary
for everything else.
The dictionary is a deliberate extension hatch, where interventions, attribute
builders, clinical transitions and observation models each own a small set of
documented keys which the engine never inspects.
A fully typed core would couple the individual to the state shape of every
intervention, and would break the dose-label namespacing that allows
multi-dose vaccination schedules to coexist.

# Composability {#sec-composability}

Within the package, composability rests largely on the competing-risks
resolution of the third stage.
Because every risk source is resolved on the same per-pair surface,
interventions usually stack without any need for pairwise interaction logic.
Isolation contributes a truncation of the transmission hazard, contact tracing
an earlier truncation for traced contacts and ring vaccination a reduction in
susceptibility, and a contact is infected if it survives all of them.
Cases that would otherwise require explicit handling, such as a contact that is
both traced and vaccinated, or a case isolated before its vaccine takes effect,
follow from the ordering of the times and the product of the survival terms.
Heterogeneity composes on a separate axis, where multiple types (age groups,
risk groups or spatial patches) enter in the offspring draw while interventions
and output need no changes because they read individual-level state.
Observation composes on a third, as an observation model returns a transformed
distribution of the latent chain-size law, and travels the same likelihood
path as the latent law without needing a likelihood method of its own.

Across packages, composition works through Turing.jl submodels
[CITE: Turing; Fjelde 2025].
The connection to the renewal-process modelling in EpiAware.jl
[CITE: EpiAware] follows from a mathematical identity, namely that the renewal
equation is the mean of a branching process with Poisson offspring.
A branching process can therefore be exposed as an EpiAware epidemic model
whose latent incidence is the renewal projection of its offspring distribution
and generation interval, after which the latent and observation models of
EpiAware apply unchanged, for example a random walk on $\log R(t)$, a
negative-binomial observation with a reporting delay and NUTS over the whole
model.
Moreover, the same identity provides a free consistency check, as one can
simulate
the individual-level process, aggregate it to incidence and compare the result
against the renewal mean.
Composition in the other direction requires no adaptor at all.
Because the analytical chain-size likelihoods are exposed as distributions, an
individual-level or outbreak-level likelihood can be added to a
population-level Turing model with `@addlogprob!`.
This is what a joint fit of community incidence and household line lists
requires, with a single shared time-varying reproduction number, community
infectious pressure entering the household model as an external hazard, and a
household contribution scored through the same objects that were used to
simulate it.
At the same time, the one family of models that we do not attempt to provide
here is that of time-varying parameters with their own process priors, which is
the domain of EpiAware and which we borrow through the bridge rather than
reimplement.

We reviewed the design against a set of composability requirements drawn up for
a wider Julia modelling programme.
The separation of concerns, the per-individual heterogeneity, the single
specification behind simulation and inference and the analytical/simulation
duality as a means of validation all hold up.
However, three requirements are not met.
Components carry structure but not priors, so parameters are fixed inputs while
priors live in the Turing model written by the user.
There is no hierarchical primitive for partial pooling across groups, and
nothing first-class for composition with machine-learning components such as
neural networks or Gaussian processes.
Nesting is also somewhat uneven, as route windows, the treatment of a household
as a window and multi-type offspring each provide a form of it without there
being a uniform rule that any model may occupy any slot.

# Analytical and simulation duality {#sec-duality}

Where a closed form exists we use it, simulation covers the remaining cases,
and the two are kept consistent.

We extend the simulation side through the model and intervention protocols
described above.
The analytical side dispatches on the existing model types and adds no new
abstract type.
Two kinds of extension plug in.
*Offspring specifications* replace what a branching process draws for each
individual, for example by letting the offspring parameters vary from chain to
chain.
They participate in simulation through the offspring draw and in the
analytical path by returning a chain-size distribution.
*Observation models* capture how the latent process gives rise to data and
return a transformed distribution of the latent chain-size law.
We write each of them once, as a transform, and on the simulation side the same
object marks the observed cases on a finished run.
Some combinations have closed forms.
Poisson offspring with a Gamma-distributed rate, for example, gives the
Gamma-Borel law used by `epichains`
[CITE: Borel; Farrington gborel; epichains], and such cases specialise the
chain-size distribution on the relevant combination of types, and dispatch
picks the closed form without one having to ask for it.
The generic case falls back to quadrature and the intractable case to
simulation.

We enforce consistency between the two paths in the test suite.
Of any extension that provides both an analytical chain-size distribution and a
simulation path we expect a regression test confirming that the two agree, and
we provide a helper for writing such tests.
In practice this doubles as a debugging tool, as a discrepancy between the
closed form and the Monte Carlo estimate localises an error to one of the two
implementations of what should be a single specification.

The duality has a direct consequence for the choice of sampler.
An analytical likelihood is a deterministic scalar function of the parameters,
so it works with any automatic differentiation backend and with gradient-based
samplers such as NUTS.
A simulation-based likelihood, on the other hand, draws random numbers, so its
output is a noisy estimate and the gradient of a single realisation is not a
useful estimate of the gradient of the expected likelihood.
Gradient-free samplers such as Metropolis-Hastings or particle methods should
be used instead.
The choice between a closed form and simulation is therefore also a choice of
sampler, and the dispatch that selects the closed form wherever it exists keeps
the more efficient path available whenever a model admits it.

# Connection to survival analysis {#sec-survival}

The generation-time distribution $g(t) = h(t)/R$ is the normalised
infectiousness profile and its CDF $G(t)$ is the cumulative hazard.
If isolation occurs at time $t_{\mathrm{iso}}$, the probability that
transmission has already occurred is $G(t_{\mathrm{iso}})$ and the probability
that it has not is $1 - G(t_{\mathrm{iso}})$, that is the transmission process
is right-censored at the time of isolation.
These are exactly the quantities computed in the timing and competing-risks
stages.
The same two objects, the generation-time distribution and the censoring time,
appear in the pairwise likelihood of @kenah2008 and @kenah2011 and in the
dynamic survival analysis of @khudabukhsh2020, and inference built on this
framework fits the same quantities that it simulates from.
The generation-time distribution also connects the individual scale to the
population growth rate through the Euler-Lotka equation $R = 1/M_g(-r)$
[@wallinga2007], where $M_g$ is the moment-generating function of $g$.

The survival view generalises the three stages beyond a single offspring law
and a single generation-time distribution.
Composing a *host timeline*, that is the disease layer understood as a sequence
of timed states running from infection through infectiousness, symptom onset,
severe disease, death or recovery and burial, lets us treat transmission as a
set of *route windows* keyed off that timeline.
A route window consists of an offspring law, a `from` state at which
infectiousness begins, the states that end it and a survival kernel for the
timing within it.
Because the timeline is a separate layer, the `from` state of a window is
resolved against the composed disease.

A number of mechanisms then become variants of the same window.
A funeral route runs between death and burial
[CITE: Weitz & Dushoff post-death Ebola], a nosocomial route between admission
and discharge, and isolation lowering $R$ becomes a route cut short by a
removal state.
The community route is the simplest window, running from infection with no
censoring, and recovers the basic model unchanged.
The latent period becomes the transition from infection to infectiousness, the
generation interval is derived from the latent period plus the kernel draw, and
isolation truncation becomes one removal state alongside death, recovery and
burial.

The generalisation lands entirely in the timing and competing-risks stages,
leaving the offspring draw as the pure, analysable layer.
$R$ remains the intrinsic reproduction number that a case would generate if
never removed, and the realised reproduction number follows from the censoring,
as shortening the infectious window blocks more contacts and lowers it.
The dispersion $k$ remains the intrinsic offspring dispersion and is
deliberately kept separate from the shape of the infectious period.
A count is never drawn from a duration, which would couple the offspring draw
to timing and break the decoupling on which the engine rests.
A window contributes contacts only once its `from` state has occurred, so a
survivor never materialises funeral contacts and nothing is created only to be
censored.
The offspring law that drives outbreak size is therefore a mixture over fates,
with community offspring for everyone and funeral offspring for the fraction
who die.
This stays closed-form where each branch is negative binomial and falls back to
simulation otherwise, and the duality described in @sec-duality carries over to
the generalised model.

The same construction extends to structure at a smaller scale.
A household can be treated as one route window scoped to a clique, with a
contact-interval kernel as the window kernel and the infectious period as its
censoring, which is how a household- or metapopulation-structured model
elsewhere in the ecosystem can reuse these survival objects
[CITE: Ball 1997 households; House & Keeling 2009].

# Discussion

EpiBranch.jl covers the individual-level stochastic and network paradigms.
We deliberately leave compartmental models and general agent-based models out
of scope, as both are already well served in Julia, the former by the
differential-equation ecosystem [CITE: DifferentialEquations.jl / SciML] and
the latter by Agents.jl [CITE: Agents.jl], whose natural unit of specification
is an individual decision rule in a space.
The intervention layer here sits above individual rules, as a policy is
generally a function of population state that modifies transmission
probabilities, delays and statuses.
In a branching process in which individuals neither move nor interact
spatially, a scheduler and a space add relatively little, whereas a minimal
stepping function keeps the offspring draw an analysable object.

Each of the three requirements that are not met in @sec-composability is an
open problem that maps onto ongoing development.
Components currently carry structure alone, and priors live in the Turing model
written by the user.
Carrying a default prior alongside the structure of a component would allow a
composed model to be sampled from directly, and would make the prior
predictive a property of the composition itself.
There is no hierarchical primitive, so one has to write partial pooling across
groups by hand in the enclosing model, for example where schools, households or
districts share a reproduction number with group-level deviations.
Nor is there anything first-class for composition with learned components, in
which a neural network or Gaussian process supplies a rate or a delay
distribution.
Beyond this, a modelling language above the Julia API would be a further step,
and one with a specific motivation, as a small validated vocabulary is a more
tractable target for automated model construction than a general-purpose API,
and the
tutorials that are checked at build time together with the duality regression
tests already give such a layer something to validate against.

The wider aim is a set of composable components for infectious disease
modelling in Julia in which the scale at which a question is posed does not
determine which package can answer it.
The bridge to EpiAware is a first instance of this, as the offspring
distribution and generation interval that drive an individual-level simulation
with interventions also define the renewal projection that is fitted to
aggregate incidence, and a household likelihood can enter the same joint model.
The composability requirements against which we reviewed the design were drawn
up for that wider programme, and the gaps they expose in priors, pooling and
learned components are gaps across it.
